Hannover Rück is a global reinsurer that backs a wide range of property and casualty risks, including cyber and digital exposures, alongside a sizeable life and health book. Hamilton Insurance Group (HG)

Hamilton Insurance Group writes specialty insurance and reinsurance worldwide, with about US$3.2b of premium across property, specialty and casualty lines, including cyber coverage, and the stock is valued at roughly US$3.7b in market cap.

"Greater use of technology and AI tools for tasks such as submission ingestion, data extraction and smart queuing in Hamilton Select is expected to improve underwriting efficiency and could affect both expense ratios and net earnings over time."

data.title: What Tamarack Valley Energy Doubters Missed
data.description:
If you had put money into Tamarack Valley Energy on 20 November 2025 and simply left it alone for a year, the outcome was striking. Holding Tamarack Valley Energy over the past year would have returned 55.4%, including dividends. That kind of move naturally tempts you to see the Clearwater story as straightforward. Yet early buyers were weighing heavy-oil concentration, ESG pressure, and rich implied P/E multiples. If you were deciding on that date, which of those trade offs would have mattered most to you?

The Two Stories Tamarack Valley Energy Investors Faced

The shares cost CA$7.35 at the start of the period, so any view on Tamarack Valley Energy began with whether that tag already reflected Clearwater potential or still underpriced it.

The bullish Narrative saw Fair Value at CA$8, about 9% above the start price, built on global energy demand and underinvestment supporting a long reserve life. That view leaned on assumptions such as revenue rising 8.2% a year to CA$1.8b by 2028 while the P/E expanded to 46.1x.

The bearish Narrative put Fair Value at CA$5.96, around 19% below the start level, and focused on ESG mandates and renewables steadily eroding oil demand. Under that script, revenue was expected to fall 3.1% a year to CA$1.3b by 2028 while the P/E moved to 32.4x and margins compressed.

What The Evidence Did To The Tamarack Valley Energy Argument

The biggest plot twist came from Tamarack Valley Energy becoming a pure play Clearwater producer through the Charlie Lake sale and the all stock Headwater merger, which leaned toward the bullish concentration thesis. At the same time, Q3 2026 told a cleaner story. Revenue moved from CA$335.8m to CA$365.8m and a prior loss turned into CA$98.8m of profit, with net margin shifting from -74.1% to 27.0%. Overall, the evidence cut both ways but tilted optimistic.

The key lesson is simple. When a thesis hangs on capital redeployment and asset focus, you test it later against segment mix, balance sheet leverage, and net margin, not just production headlines.

What Tamarack Valley Energy's Run Still Leaves You To Judge

Tamarack Valley Energy now trades at CA$11.65 after a 55.4% gain over the past year. The analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St sees Fair Value above that level based on its Clearwater heavy oil focus.

The Narrative leans on Clearwater waterflood expansion, the Headwater combination and a debt free balance sheet. It argues today's price still does not fully credit the potential for lower decline rates and cash generation from the enlarged Clearwater position.

"The move to a debt free balance sheet with over $500 million of cash and an undrawn $875 million credit facility gives Tamarack Valley Energy more room to keep funding Clearwater growth, buybacks and rising base dividends from internal cash generation, which ties back to net income and free funds flow."

Oil production needs pipes, storage and gas networks that keep molecules moving. Another business focuses on that kind of fee based infrastructure.

Its assets move crude, move gas and house energy in underground storage. Large expansion projects aim to add more regulated and contracted capacity.

Government approval of the revised Rovuma concept and the push toward a final investment decision by the end of 2026 turn this from a distant concept into a live project risk and opportunity. LunaRodas pins fair value at US$180.96 for ExxonMobil, arguing that the current mix of disciplined dividend growth, the US$20b buyback commitment, and visible execution on Guyana, Permian automation, and Rovuma LNG provides enough clarity on future cash generation to justify that valuation anchor.

Many investors haven't heard of the accrual ratio from cashflow, but it is actually a useful measure of how well a company's profit is backed up by free cash flow (FCF) during a given period. In plain english, this ratio subtracts FCF from net profit, and divides that number by the company's average operating assets over that period. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. While having an accrual ratio above zero is of little concern, we do think it's worth noting when a company has a relatively high accrual ratio. Notably, there is some academic evidence that suggests that a high accrual ratio is a bad sign for near-term profits, generally speaking.
